title: Blessing your children
hookLine: hands on heads each Friday night
tomorrow: the Torah says when to teach your kids. hint: not at a desk.

cards: A hand on top of the head is how people check for a fever, how a coach says good game, how a grandparent says hello without words.
On Friday night, before the meal, some Jewish parents rest their hands on their children's heads and say a few lines from the Torah. Whose words are they, and why those?

teach.b: For sons, the words come from Genesis. Old Jacob, his eyes dim, is blessing his grandsons, Joseph's two boys, and he says Israel will bless its children with their names: "God make thee as Ephraim and as Manasseh."
For daughters, a custom names the four mothers: may God make you like Sarah, Rebekah, Rachel and Leah.

Then some families add the blessing the priests gave in the Temple, from the book of Numbers: "The LORD bless thee, and keep thee; The LORD make His face to shine upon thee, and be gracious unto thee; The LORD lift up His countenance upon thee, and give thee peace."

Why Ephraim and Manasseh, and not Abraham or Moses? One reading: they're brothers in Genesis who don't fight, and they grew up far from home, in Egypt, and stayed who they were. Now notice the senses in it.
The weight of a hand. A parent's voice close enough to hear the breath. Some parents add a few quiet words of their own.
And nothing has to be earned first: the hands come on a bad week too.
Something to tell a friend: the blessing for sons is named for two grandsons, blessed by their grandfather.

how: On Friday night, before Kiddush, some parents place their hands on each child's head and say the blessing: Ephraim and Manasseh for sons, Sarah, Rebekah, Rachel and Leah for daughters; some add the priestly blessing from Numbers 6.

games.q: a friend's kid had a rough week: detention, a slammed door. on Friday she wonders whether to skip the blessing 'until he earns it.' what fits the custom?
o: bless him anyway; the hands come on a hard week too.
skip it this week, so he learns that blessings are rewards.
bless only the sibling who behaved, to make a point.
games.why: the blessing isn't a grade. it's Friday night, hands on heads, every week, earned or not.

practice: Rest one hand lightly on the top of your own head, or on the head of a child you love if one is beside you. Feel its weight, warm and still. Bring one child in your life to mind by name.
If you pray, you can say the priests' words from Numbers for them; if not, simply hold them in mind under that hand.

carryVoice: Keep this one close: hands on heads, on a good week and a hard one. Five days into home and family.
